standards.title: Financial Accounting Standard No. (4): Musharaka Financing
linked_standards: Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions

standards.applicability: Applies to Musharaka financing transactions carried out by Islamic banks, whether constant (short or long-term) or diminishing Musharaka, whether funded from the bank's own funds, from a pool commingled with unrestricted investment accounts, or from restricted investment accounts, and to the bank's share in Musharaka profits or losses (para. 1); excludes Mudaraba, Participations, Zakah on Musharaka funds, and the accounting treatment of Musharaka transactions in the partner's (client's) books and the Musharaka records (para. 2).

Accounting Treatment of Musharaka Financing (paras 3-16): 2/1 Recognition of the Islamic bank's share in Musharaka capital at contracting (para 3, p.232); 2/2 Measurement at time of contracting (paras 4-6, p.233); 2/3 Measurement after contracting at end of financial period (paras 7-10, p.233-234); 2/4 Recognition of profit/loss (paras 11-16, p.234-235); 2/5 Disclosure requirements (paras 17-18, p.235); 3. Effective Date (para 19, p.235); Adoption of the Standard (p.236, Board meeting No.10); Appendix (A) Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard (p.237-240); Appendix (B) Juristic Rules for Musharaka Financing Transactions (p.241-250): 1. Definition of Musharaka in Fiqh; 1/1 Categories (Al-'Inan, Al-Mufawada, Al-A'mal, Al-Wujuh); 1/2 Elements and conditions; 1/3 Rules (capital, work, profit, loss, termination); Appendix (C) Reasons for the Standard (p.251-252); Appendix (D) Basis for Conclusions (cites para. 36, para. 112, para. 98, Statement of Concepts para. 74, Statement of Objectives para. 33) (p.253-254); Appendix (E) Definitions: Musharaka, Constant Musharaka, Diminishing Musharaka, Participation, Mudaraba (p.255-256).
key_points: Standard applies to Musharaka financing carried out by Islamic banks, whether constant (short or long-term) or diminishing Musharaka (para. 1).

Applies whether the Islamic bank funds its Musharaka share exclusively from its own funds, from a pool commingled with unrestricted investment accounts, or from restricted investment accounts, and to the bank's share in Musharaka profits or losses (para. 1).
Any contradiction between the standard and the Islamic bank's charter or the laws/regulations of its operating country must be disclosed (para. 1).
Standard excludes Mudaraba, Participations, Zakah on Musharaka funds, and accounting treatment of Musharaka transactions in the partner's (client's) books and Musharaka records (para. 2).

Islamic bank's share in Musharaka capital (cash or kind) is recognized when paid to the partner or made available to him on account of the Musharaka, presented under a Musharaka Financing account (para. 3).
Cash contribution measured by the amount paid or made available to the partner on account of the Musharaka (para. 4).

In-kind contribution (trading assets or non-monetary assets) measured at fair value agreed between the partners; difference between fair value and book value recognized as profit or loss to the Islamic bank (para. 5).
Contracting-procedure expenses (e.g., feasibility studies) are not part of Musharaka capital unless otherwise agreed by both parties (para. 6).
Islamic bank's share in constant Musharaka capital measured at period end at historical cost (the amount paid or the value of the asset at contracting) (para. 7).

Islamic bank's share in diminishing Musharaka measured at period end at historical cost less the historical cost of any share transferred to the partner (transfer via sale at fair value); the difference between historical cost and fair value is recognized as profit or loss (para. 8).

If a diminishing Musharaka is liquidated before complete transfer, the amount recovered is credited to the Musharaka financing account, with any resulting profit or loss (book value vs. recovered amount) recognized in the income statement (para. 9).
If the Musharaka is terminated or liquidated and the bank's due share remains unpaid at settlement, it is recognized as a receivable due from the partner (para. 10).
Profits/losses on Musharaka transactions that commence and end within one financial period are recognized at the time of liquidation (para. 11).

For a constant Musharaka spanning more than one financial period, the bank's profit share is recognized to the extent it is being distributed; loss share is recognized to the extent it is being deducted from the bank's Musharaka capital share (para. 12).

The same treatment (item 2/4/2) applies to a diminishing Musharaka spanning more than one financial period, after considering the decline in the bank's capital share and its profits/losses (para. 13).
If the partner does not pay the bank's due share of profits after liquidation or settlement, it is recognized as a receivable due from the partner (para. 14).
Losses caused by the partner's misconduct or negligence are borne by the partner and recognized as a receivable due from the partner (para. 15).
Unpaid amounts under items 2/3/4 and 2/4/4 are recorded in a Musharaka receivables account; a provision is made if the receivables are doubtful (para. 16).
Disclosure required in the notes to financial statements if the Islamic bank made a provision during the period for a loss of its Musharaka capital (para. 17).

The disclosure requirements of Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions must be observed (para. 18).
Standard effective for financial statements for fiscal periods beginning 1 Muharram 1418 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 1998 A.D. (para. 19).

Musharaka defined in fiqh as the commingling of funds for the purpose of sharing in profit; partnerships divide into Holding Partnership and Contract Partnership, with contract partnerships further divided into Al-'Inan, Al-Mufawada, Al-A'mal and Al-Wujuh (Appendix B, 1 and 1/1).
General rules of profit: profit must be quantifiable, and each partner's profit must be a proportionate share of total partnership profit, not a predetermined fixed amount (Appendix B, 1/3/3(a)).

Fuqaha agree that losses must be divided strictly in proportion to each partner's capital contribution ("Wadhi'ah"), citing Ali Ibn Abu Talib: loss should be proportionate to funds contributed (Appendix B, 1/3/4).

Neither partner can guarantee the other partner's capital because Musharaka rests on Al-Ghurm Bil-Ghunm (entitlement to return tied to exposure to risk); a partner may still require guarantees against the other's negligence or misconduct (Appendix B, 1/3/1(b)).
divergence_notes: Al-'Inan partnership: "Hanafis and Hanbalis allow ... profits of the two parties to be divided in proportion to their contributed funds; profits may be divided equally but contributed funds may be different; and profits may be unequally divided, but contributed funds are equal"; "Malikis and Shafis make the acceptance of this type of partnership conditional on profits and losses being proportionate to the size of contributions to the overall fund because ... profit ... is considered to be return on capital" (Appendix B, 1/1/1).

Commingling of funds: "Shafis and Malikis argue that the funds provided by partners should be commingled in order that no privilege be given to the share of either of them. However, Hanafis do not stipulate this condition provided the capital is in cash, while the Hanbalis do not require commingling of funds" (Appendix B, 1/2/2/3(a)).

Rules of allocating profit among partners, two opinions: "First: Profit should be divided among the partners in proportion to their contributed capital ... This is the opinion of Malikis and Shafis"; "Second: Profit may vary between the partners if it is so provided for in the contract. This is the opinion of Hanafis and Hanbalis" (Appendix B, 1/3/3(b)).

Musharaka termination: "The majority of Fuqaha, except for Malikis, are of the opinion that ... each of the partners is entitled to terminate it whenever he wishes, as is the case with agency contracts" (Appendix B, 1/3/5).

Status of Mudaraba as a partnership: "Fuqaha have differed on whether Mudaraba is a partnership in this sense or not. Some Fuqaha consider Mudaraba to be such a partnership ... Others, however, do not consider Mudaraba to be one of the types of contract partnership" (Appendix B, 1/1).

standards.title: Financial Accounting Standard No. (7): Salam and Parallel Salam
standards.effective_date: 1999-01-01 (fiscal periods beginning 1 Muharram 1419 A.H. or 1 January 1999 A.D.) (para 21)
linked_standards: Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
Statement of Financial Accounting No. (1): Objectives of Financial Accounting for Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
Statement of Financial Accounting No. (2): Concepts of Financial Accounting for Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
standards.applicability: Applies to accounting for Salam financing and parallel Salam transactions carried out by Islamic banks and financial institutions, including Ra`s Al-Mal paid/received, receipt and sale/delivery of Al-Muslam Fihi, and related revenues, expenses, gains and losses (para 1). If the standard's requirements conflict with the Islamic bank's charter or the laws/regulations of its country of operation, the point of conflict must be disclosed (para 1).
standards.structure: Preface (aims of standard). Statement of the Standard (paras 1-21): 1. Scope of the Standard (para 1); 2. Accounting Treatments of Salam Financing and Parallel Salam Transactions (paras 2-19), with subsections 2/1 recognition of Salam financing, 2/2 recognition of parallel Salam, 2/3 measurement at contracting, 2/4 measurement at period end, 2/5 receipt of Al-Muslam Fihi (2/5/1-2/5/4), 2/6 substitution, 2/7 post-receipt period-end measurement, 2/8 recognition of result of delivery in parallel Salam; 3. Disclosure Requirements (para 20); 4. Effective Date (para 21). Adoption of the Standard (Board meeting No. 13, 15-16 June 1997). Appendix (A): Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard. Appendix (B): Juristic Rules of Salam and Parallel Salam - 1. Definition; 2. Legitimacy (2/1-2/3); 3. Capital of Salam (3/1-3/2/2); 4. Al-Muslam Fihi (4/1-4/9, incl. 4/8 Sale of Al-Muslam Fihi before receiving it, 4/9 Replacement/substitution); 5. Parallel Salam (5/1-5/2); 6. General Rules - nullification/cancellation (6/1), delivery before/on due date (6/2/1-6/2/5); 7. Options if Al-Muslam Fihi unavailable on due date (7/1-7/2); 8. Transfer/pledge of Al-Muslam Fihi as guarantee. Appendix (C): Reasons for the Standard. Appendix (D): Basis for Conclusions. Appendix (E): Definitions.
key_points: Salam financing is recognized when the capital of Salam (in cash, kind or benefit) is paid or made available to Al-Muslam Ileihi (para 2).
Parallel Salam transactions are recognized when the Islamic bank receives the capital of Salam in cash, kind, or benefit (para 3).
At the time of contracting, capital is measured by the amount paid (para 4).
Capital provided in kind or benefit is measured at the fair value agreed between the Islamic bank and the client (para 5).
If it is probable Al-Muslam Ileihi will not deliver Al-Muslam Fihi in full or in part, or its value will decline, the Islamic bank makes a provision for the amount of the estimated deficit (para 6).
Salam financing transactions are presented in the financial statements under the heading 'Salam Financing' (para 7).
Parallel Salam transactions are presented as a liability under the heading 'Parallel Salam' (para 8).
Assets constitutive of Al-Muslam Fihi received under the contract are recorded at their historical cost (para 9).
Where received Al-Muslam Fihi is of different quality but equal market/fair value to the contracted value, it is measured and recorded at book value (para 10).

Where the market/fair value of received Al-Muslam Fihi is lower than the book value of the contracted Al-Muslam Fihi, it is recorded at market/fair value and the difference is recognized as a loss (para 11).
If delivery is extended after complete or partial failure to receive Al-Muslam Fihi at the due date, the book value remains as it is (para 12).
If the Salam contract is completely or partially cancelled and the client does not repay the capital, the amount is recognized as a receivable due from the client (para 13).
Where failure to deliver is due to the client's misconduct or negligence and the contract is cancelled without repayment, the amount due is recognized as a receivable from the client (para 14).

Where pledged securities against Al-Muslam Fihi are sold for less than book value, the difference is a receivable from the client; if sold for more, the difference is credited to the client (para 15).
The client is debited with any additional amounts established in favour of the Islamic bank (para 16).
Substitution of another kind of goods for Al-Muslam Fihi follows the same loss-recognition treatment as item 2/5/2/2 when the substitute's market/fair value is less than book value (para 17).
After receipt, at period end, assets acquired through Salam financing are measured at the lower of historical cost and cash equivalent value, with any decline recognized as a loss (para 18).

Upon delivery of Al-Muslam Fihi by the Islamic bank to the client in a parallel Salam transaction, the difference between the amount paid by the client and the cost of Al-Muslam Fihi is recognized as profit or loss (para 19).
Disclosure requirements follow Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions (para 20).
The Standard is effective for financial statements for fiscal periods beginning 1 Muharram 1419 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 1999 A.D. (para 21).
Salam financing represented about 5% of total finance provided by the Islamic banks participating in the AAOIFI-commissioned empirical study, used mainly in the agriculture sector (Appendix C).

Salam is defined as purchase of a commodity for deferred delivery in exchange for immediate payment according to specified conditions, or sale of a commodity for deferred delivery in exchange for immediate payment (Appendix E, Definitions).

divergence_evidence.topic: Sale of Al-Muslam Fihi before receiving it
divergence_evidence.position: AAOIFI (Appendix B - Juristic Rules of Salam and Parallel Salam): Al-Muslam Fihi is subject to specification and can be recognized as a debt (Appendix B 4/1). The majority of Fuqaha consider it impermissible to sell Al-Muslam Fihi before receiving it, based on the rule preventing the sale of food and other movable items before receipt, since earning a profit without an obligation to deliver is not permitted (Appendix B 4/8/1). The Malikis agree with the majority on prohibiting sale before receipt only where Al-Muslam Fihi is food; otherwise they permit it subject to conditions: sale back to Al-Muslam Ileihi is permitted at the contract price or lower (Appendix B 4/8/2/1), and sale to a third party is permitted at the contract price (if quality matches) or at a higher/lower price (if quality differs) (Appendix B 4/8/2/2). The Standard's Statement (paras 1-21) does not itself adopt a position on this issue; it is recorded only as a juristic-rules background in Appendix B (absent from the operative accounting rules).

divergence_notes: "Fuqaha have differed as to the permissibility of payment in the form of trading assets... Malikis have also allowed payment to be in the form of a benefit in kind, such as the benefit of living in a house" (Appendix B 3/1).
"The Malikis have permitted a short delay in making the Salam payment" (Appendix B 3/2/2).
"The Shafis have permitted prompt delivery of Salam", contrasted with the majority of Fuqaha who require delivery to be deferred (Appendix B 4/3/1-4/3/2).

"Fuqaha have differed on the issue of the lack of specificity that is considered permissible with regard to the delivery date of Al-Muslam Fihi"; the majority require greater specificity, but the Malikis (and one Hanbali version) consider a range of possible delivery dates acceptable, which is the view adopted in this standard (Appendix B 4/4).

The Shari'a supervisory board of Al Rajhi Banking and Investment Corporation issued Fatwa No. (41) permitting parallel Salam on condition the second contract's execution is not made dependent on the first (Appendix B 5/1).

"Some contemporary Fuqaha have prohibited parallel Salam, particularly if it is for the purpose of trading and such a transaction becomes recurrent, as this may be suspected as involving Riba" (Appendix B 5/2).
"The majority of Fuqaha have prohibited the replacement of Al-Muslam Fihi before it is received except by substituting another kind of similar goods" (Appendix B 4/9/1).

The Malikis permit replacement of Al-Muslam Fihi by substitution where it is not food, based on their school's view permitting sale of goods before receipt, differing from the majority (Appendix B 4/9/2).
Some contemporary Fuqaha hold substitution permissible whether or not Al-Muslam Fihi is food, subject to conditions on kind-suitability and quantity (Appendix B 4/9/3).
"Fuqaha have differed on whether or not it is considered permissible for Al-Muslam Ileihi to deliver a different type of Al-Muslam Fihi than the one agreed upon" (Appendix B 6/2/4).

standards.title: Financial Accounting Standard No. (9): Zakah
linked_standards: Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
Statement of Financial Accounting No. (1): Objectives of Financial Accounting for Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
Statement of Financial Accounting No. (2): Concepts of Financial Accounting for Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
standards.applicability: Applies to the accounting treatments related to determination of the Zakah base, measurement of items included in the Zakah base, and disclosure of Zakah in the financial statements of the Islamic bank; Appendix (A) is an integral part of the standard (para 1); the Islamic bank must refer to its Shari'a supervisory board on Zakah issues not covered by the standard (Preface); where the standard's requirements conflict with the bank's charter or the laws/regulations of its country, the point of conflict must be disclosed (para 1).
standards.structure: Preface. Statement of the Standard (paras 1-21): 1. Scope of the Standard (1); 2. Accounting Treatment of Zakah Base (2-12) - 2/1 Determination of Zakah base (2-8): 2/1/1 Net assets method (3-6), 2/1/2 Net invested funds method (7-8); 2/2 Treatment of Zakah in the financial statements (9-12): 2/2/1 Cases obliged to pay Zakah (9), 2/2/2 Cases not obliged to pay Zakah (10-11), 2/2/3 Presentation in statement of sources and uses of funds in Zakah and charity fund (12); 3. Disclosure Requirements (13-20, items 3/1-3/8); 4. Effective Date (21). Adoption of the Standard. Appendix (A) Example of Items Included in Determining the Zakah Base. Appendix (B) Example Illustrating How to Determine the Zakah Base. Appendix (C) Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard. Appendix (D) Juristic Rules for Zakah (Preface; Definition of Zakah; Conditions for Liability to Zakah; Duplication of Zakah; Tax; Zakah on Unlawful/Suspect Funds; Conditions of Zakah on Trading Assets; Valuation of Trading Assets; Payment from Same Goods or Value; Zakah on Debts Owed by Third Parties; Debt (Liabilities); Zakah on Other Types of Assets; Zakah on Livestock; Zakah on Agricultural and Horticultural Produce; Gains; Methods of Determining the Zakah Base). Appendix (E) Reasons for the Standard. Appendix (F) Basis for Conclusions. Appendix (G) Definitions.
key_points: Standard applies to accounting treatments for determination of the Zakah base, measurement of items in the base, and disclosure of Zakah in financial statements of Islamic banks (para 1).
Zakah base determined using 2.5% for a lunar calendar year and 2.5775% for a solar calendar year, using either the Net Assets method or the Net Invested Funds method (para 2).

Net assets method: Zakah base = assets subject to Zakah – (liabilities due to be paid during the year + equity of unrestricted investment accounts + minority interest + equity owned by government, endowment, charity, and not-for-profit organizations excluding individually-owned equity) (para 3).

Assets subject to Zakah include cash and cash equivalent, receivables net of provisions for doubtful debts, trading assets (inventory, marketable securities, real estate, etc.), and financing assets (Mudaraba, Musharaka, Salam, Istisna'a) net of provisions for fall in value or non-collectability; funds used to acquire fixed assets relating to financing assets are deducted (para 4).
Assets acquired for trading are measured at their cash equivalent value on the date Zakah is due (para 5).
For assets available for trading in the form of agricultural products or livestock (camels, cows, sheep, goats), the Shari'a-prescribed rates and Nisab specified for such assets apply (para 6).

Net invested funds method: Zakah base = paid-up capital + reserves + provisions not deducted from assets + retained earnings + net income + liabilities not due during the year – (net fixed assets + investments not acquired for trading + accumulated losses) (para 7).
The two methods are strictly equivalent provided items are classified and valued consistently, given the different valuation bases used (paras 2, 8).

Zakah is treated as a non-operating expense in the income statement when: the law requires payment, the charter/by-laws require it, or the general assembly passes a resolution requiring it; unpaid Zakah is presented as a liability in the statement of financial position (para 9).
Where shareholders ask the bank to act as agent from distributable profits, Zakah is deducted from the shareholders' share of distributable profits (para 10).
Where the bank agrees to act as agent even with insufficient distributable profits, the amount paid is recorded as a receivable due from those shareholders (para 11).
Zakah due from the bank and Zakah received from other sources are presented in the statement of sources and uses of funds in the Zakah and charity fund (para 12).

Disclosure required in the notes of: the method used to determine the Zakah base and items included (para 13); Shari'a supervisory board rulings on Zakah issues not covered by the standard (para 14); whether the bank as a holding company pays its share of Zakah for subsidiaries (para 15); the amount of Zakah due from each share if the bank does not pay Zakah (para 16); the amount of Zakah due from the equity of investment accountholders (para 17); whether the bank collects/pays Zakah on behalf of investment account holders and others (para 18); restrictions set by the Shari'a supervisory board in determining the Zakah base, e.g. under the net invested funds method total net fixed assets plus non-trading investments should not exceed total paid-up capital plus reserves (para 19); FAS No. (1) disclosure requirements also apply (para 20).
Standard effective for financial statements for fiscal periods beginning 1 Muharram 1420 A.H. or 1 January 1999 A.D. (para 21).

Nisab for gold is 85 grams of gold; Nisab for silver is 595 grams of silver; Nisab for cash and trading goods is estimated using their cash equivalent compared to the value of gold (Appendix D, Attainment of the Nisab).

Hawl is the passing of a lunar calendar year from the day Nisab is attained; decreases during the year are ignored for Nisab purposes; solar-calendar users apply an increased rate of 2.5775% instead of 2.5% to compensate for the calendar difference (Appendix D, Passing of Hawl).

Nisab for agricultural/horticultural produce is five Awsuq (unit equal to 653 kg of wheat or the like); Zakah rate is 10% (one tenth) where irrigated by natural rainwater, 5% (half of one tenth) where irrigated by machinery, and 7.5% (three quarters of one tenth) where irrigation combines both methods (Appendix D, Zakah on Agricultural and Horticultural Produce).
Livestock Zakah (camels, cows, sheep, goats) requires attainment of the prescribed Nisab, passing of Hawl, and that the animals not be used as work animals (Appendix D, Zakah on Livestock).

Debt (Liabilities): the standard adopts the Shafi view that debt payable now or in future should not be deducted from assets subject to Zakah for medium/long-term debt; only debt due to be paid during the year following the statement-of-financial-position date is deducted (Appendix D, Debt (Liabilities)).

Zakah on receivables (debts owed by third parties): due where the debtor acknowledges and can pay, or evidence shows the debt is due and collectible; where collectability is doubtful, Zakah is payable only on the amount recovered, and only once at the time of recovery, not for the years the amount remained outstanding (Appendix D, Zakah on Debts Owed by Third Parties).

Trading assets are valued for Zakah at market selling price (cash equivalent value), not historical cost, so the Zakah base includes historical cost plus any holding gains or losses (Appendix D, Valuation of Trading Assets).

Cash and cash equivalents for Zakah purposes include, in addition to local/foreign currency and on-demand deposits, gold and silver in the form of currencies, bullion and others (Appendix G, Definitions).
Worked example: Zakah base of $128,094,035 is calculated identically under both methods; Zakah for the period = $128,094,035 x 2.5775% = $3,301,624 (Appendix B).
divergence_notes: "According to the majority of Fuqaha, debt that is payable during the current or future financial periods should be deducted from assets subject to Zakah. However, the Shafi are of the view that any debt payable whether now or in future should not be deducted...In this standard, we have adopted the view of the Shafi school" (Appendix D, Debt (Liabilities)).

"This is the position of the Hanafi school that was also adopted in the First Conference on Zakah" — regarding treating the passing of Hawl as a lunar year from the day Nisab is attained (Appendix D, Passing of Hawl (year)).

"The Maliki jurists make a distinction between trading assets held for sale at the current market price and those held in expectation of selling them at a specific price in the future...However, the majority of jurists do not make this distinction" (Appendix D, Conditions of Zakah on Trading Assets).

"The majority of jurists have stipulated the condition that animals liable to Zakah should be freely grazing for most of the year, without being fed fodder. The Malikis, however, did not stipulate this condition" (Appendix D, Zakah on Livestock).

"According to the Hanafis, Zakah is payable on all crops that grow on land...Other Schools of Fiqh have their own details and conditions on what is subject to Zakah from agricultural and horticultural produce" (Appendix D, Zakah on Agricultural and Horticultural Produce).
"This is the opinion of the Hanafis, and this is a safe way as a compromise between the divergent views as to the different times when Zakah is due on gains" (Appendix D, Gains).

Characterisation of Istisna’a, 2. Definition, 3. Legitimacy of Istisna’a (3/1-3/3), 4. Conditions for Validity (4/1 Al-Masnoo’, 4/2 Price), 5. Binding Nature of Istisna’a (5/1-5/5), 6. Legal Consequences, 7. Guarantee, 8. Penalty Clause, 9. Options on Non-Compliance, 10. Termination, 11. Parallel Istisna’a, plus Salam/Istisna’a comparison table (p.388-396). Appendix (d): Reasons for the Standard (p.397-398). Appendix (e): Basis for Conclusions (p.399-401). Appendix (f): Definitions (p.402-403).
key_points: Istisna’a costs consist of direct costs (production of Al-Masnoo’) and indirect costs allocated on an objective basis; general/administrative expenses, selling expenses and R&D costs are excluded from contract costs (para 2).

Istisna’a costs incurred during a period, plus pre-contract costs, are recognized in an Istisna’a work-in-progress account under assets; billed amounts are debited to Istisna’a accounts receivable and credited to an Istisna’a billings account, offset against work-in-progress (para 3).

Pre-contract costs are recognized as deferred costs when incurred and transferred to the work-in-progress account upon contracting; if no contract is signed and is unlikely to be, they are written off to expense in the current period (para 4).

Where a parallel Istisna’a exists, contract costs include the price fixed in the parallel contract (direct costs) plus indirect costs; subcontractor billings are debited to an Istisna’a costs account (an asset) and credited to Istisna’a accounts payable (para 5).

Progress billings to the ultimate purchaser (Al-Mustasni’) are debited to Istisna’a accounts receivable and credited to an Istisna’a billings account, offset against the Istisna’a costs account (para 6).
Istisna’a revenue is the total price agreed with Al-Mustasni’, including profit margin, recognized under either the percentage of completion or completed contract method (para 7).

Under the percentage of completion method, revenue commensurate with work performed each period is recognized, and the corresponding portion of the profit margin (cash price to purchaser less estimated total costs) is added to the work-in-progress account (paras 8-9).

The completed contract method applies only in unusual circumstances where neither percentage of completion nor cost-to-complete can be estimated with reasonable accuracy; no revenue is recognized until the contract is fully completed (para 10).

Deferred profits (difference between amounts paid during the contract and the total agreed price where price is paid after completion) are offset against Istisna’a accounts receivable, recognized either proportionately over the future credit period (preferred method) or as/when each instalment is received, the latter requiring a Shari’a supervisory board decision or supervisory-authority requirement (paras 11-13).

On early settlement, if the bank waives part of its profit for advance payment, the waived amount is deducted from both Istisna’a accounts receivable and deferred profits; the same treatment applies where the bank instead reimburses Al-Mustasni’ after receiving the payment (paras 14-15).

Parallel Istisna’a revenue and profit must be measured only under the percentage of completion method since both costs and revenues are known with reasonable certainty; the recognized profit portion is added to the Istisna’a costs account (paras 16-17).

Istisna’a work-in-progress (or the costs account in parallel Istisna’a) is measured and reported at a value not exceeding its cash equivalent value (contract price less expected additional cost to complete); any expected loss is recognized in the income statement (paras 19-21).

Additional costs arising from a subcontractor's failure to honour obligations in a parallel Istisna’a are recognized as losses in valuing the Istisna’a costs account and reported in the income statement, unless recovery is reasonably certain (para 22).

The value and cost of change orders authorized by the bank and Al-Mustasni’ are added to Istisna’a revenue and costs respectively; qualifying additional claims are recognized as revenue equal to the additional cost caused, while non-qualifying claims are disclosed in the notes (paras 23-26).

Maintenance and warranty costs of Al-Masnoo’ are accounted for on an accrual basis (estimated and matched against recognized revenue) for a direct Istisna’a contract, but on a cash basis (expensed when incurred) where a parallel Istisna’a exists (paras 27-28).

As Al-Mustasni’ (buyer), progress billings received are debited to an Istisna’a costs account under assets and credited to Istisna’a accounts payable to Al-Sani’; the same treatment applies when a parallel Istisna’a exists (paras 29-30).

Al-Masnoo’ received in conformity with specifications is recorded at the historical (book) cost of the Istisna’a costs account; where a parallel Istisna’a exists, on delivery the costs account balance transfers to an asset account reflecting the nature of Al-Masnoo’ (paras 31-32).

For late delivery due to Al-Sani’'s negligence or fault, compensation is first taken from performance bonds; any shortfall is recognized as Istisna’a accounts receivable, with an allowance for doubtful debts formed if necessary (para 33).

If the bank declines non-conforming Al-Masnoo’ and cannot recover all progress payments, the balance is recorded as Istisna’a accounts receivable (with a doubtful-debt allowance if needed); if it accepts non-conforming Al-Masnoo’, the asset is measured at the lower of cash equivalent value or historical cost, with any uncompensated loss recognized in income (paras 34-35).

If Al-Mustasni’ refuses to receive Al-Masnoo’, the Istisna’a assets are measured at the lower of cash equivalent value or historical cost, with any resulting loss recognized in income in the period the loss is realized (para 36).

Financial-statement disclosures required include: revenues/profits of Istisna’a contracts recognized for the period; accounting methods used; cumulative costs, revenues and profits recognized to date; retention amounts on contracts in progress; and receivable/payable balances presented without offsetting against each other (paras 37-41).

Notes disclosures required include: unsettled additional claims and contingent penalty-clause fines for delivery delay; the method used to determine percentage of completion; the value and time periods of parallel Istisna’a in progress; and the value and time periods of signed but not-yet-commenced Istisna’a contracts (paras 42-45).

The disclosure requirements of Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions must also be observed (para 46).
Effective date: fiscal periods beginning 1 Muharram 1420 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 1999 A.D. (para 47).
divergence_notes: Majority of Hanafi jurists hold Istisna’a is “valid but not binding”: each party may rescind before implementation, and Al-Sani’ need not deliver manufactured goods (Appendix (c), sec. 5/1, 5/1/1-5/1/2).

Three Hanafi views once Al-Sani’ manufactures Al-Masnoo’ to specification and elects to deliver: (a) preponderant view — binding on Al-Sani’ who waives his option, buyer's option remains (attributed to Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad); (b) Abu Hanifah also reported to retain an equal-footing right; (c) Abu Yusuf's second opinion — contract becomes binding on both parties (Appendix (c), sec. 5/1/3).
“The majority in the Hanafi School opined that the Istisna’a contract is binding once it has been constituted” (Appendix (c), sec. 5/2).

Provision (392) of Majallat Al-Ahkam Al-’Adliyyah: “Once the contract of Istisna’a is constituted, it becomes binding and no party has the right to revoke it,” subject to Al-Mustasni’'s option to revoke if Al-Masnoo’ does not conform to specifications; per Abu Yousuf, no party may withdraw without the other's consent (Appendix (c), sec. 5/3).

Civil legislations based on Shari’a (Jordanian, Yemeni, Sudanese laws, and the Unified Arab Law proposed by the League of Arab Countries) treat Istisna’a as a binding contract, following Majallat Al-Ahkam Al-’Adliyyah (Appendix (c), sec. 5/4).

Islamic Fiqh Academy resolution: “The contract of Istisna’a is binding on its parties provided that certain conditions are fulfilled” (Appendix (c), sec. 5/5, citing 7th Session, Resolution No. 67/3/7, 1412 A.H./1992 A.D.).

On legitimacy: Hanafis originally held Istisna’a should have been prohibited under strict Qiyas (subject-matter not in existence/possession of seller) but approved it via Istihsan grounded in continuous practice (amounting to Ijma’) and need; some contemporary Fuqaha instead hold it valid directly under Qiyas since non-existence at contracting is compensated by preponderant existence at delivery, removing Gharar (Appendix (c), sec. 3/1, 3/3).

Three Hanafi opinions on fixing a future delivery date: Abu Hanifah prohibited fixing a date (doing so converts the contract into Salam); Abu Yusuf and Muhammad Ibn Al-Hasan Al-Shaybani accepted fixing a date based on common practice; all three agree that a date not in line with common practice converts Istisna’a into Salam. The standard adopts the two companions' view that fixing a future delivery date is a necessity (Appendix (c), sec. 4/1/3).

standards.applicability: Applies to the financial statements prepared by the company (Islamic Insurance company, also called Takaful company, per fn 1) to meet the common information needs of the main users of such statements; applicable to all companies regardless of legal form, country of incorporation, or size; where standard requirements conflict with the company's charter or the laws/regulations of its country, the conflict and its impact on relevant financial statement elements should be disclosed wherever possible (para 1).

Appendix (C) Reasons for the Standard. Appendix (D) Basis for Conclusions. Appendix (E) Definitions. Appendix (F) Example of Financial Statements and Disclosures Therein.
key_points: Standard applies to financial statements of all Islamic insurance (Takaful) companies regardless of legal form, country of incorporation, or size; conflicts with charter or law must be disclosed with impact where possible (para 1).

Complete set of financial statements comprises: statement of financial position, statement of policyholders' revenues and expenses, income statement, statement of cash flows, statement of changes in owners' equity, statement of policyholders' surplus (or deficit), statement of sources and uses of funds in the Zakah and charity fund, notes, and optional supplementary statements/reports if not contradicting Shari'a rules (para 2).
Comparative amounts required as a minimum, enabling users to differentiate actual changes in financial position/results/cash flows from accounting changes (para 3).
Form, classifications, and terminology of the financial statements must ensure clear presentation and user comprehension (para 4).
Pages and notes must be numbered consecutively; notes given clear distinct titles and cross-referenced to related financial statement items (para 5).
Notes are an integral part of the financial statements; a specified statement must appear on the bottom of every page containing a financial statement (para 6).
All material information necessary for the financial statements to be adequate, relevant and reliable must be disclosed (para 7).

Basic company information disclosure (para 8) includes: name, country of incorporation, formation date/legal form, headquarters/branch locations, authorized activities and major insurance services, consolidated and non-consolidated subsidiaries with ownership percentages, holding company/affiliates, role and authority of the Shari'a supervisory board, supervising regulatory authority, and tax treatment including tax holiday period.
Disclose currency used for accounting measurement (para 9) and the method used for translating foreign currency balances and transactions (para 10).

Significant accounting policies disclosed in one note (para 12), covering as a minimum: recognition of earned contributions, outstanding claims and claims incurred but not reported, unearned contributions, insurance business acquisition cost, commission earned from reinsurers, foreign currency translation, development cost amortization, subsidiary consolidation, policies presenting a choice of acceptable alternatives, policies inconsistent with AAOIFI objectives/concepts/standards, other material revenues/gains/losses, and revaluation bases (para 13).
Disclose unusual supervisory restrictions that restrict management's decision-making ability or prevent authorized activities (para 14).

Disclose the amount and nature of earnings and expenditures not permitted by Shari'a and how the company intends to dispose of assets generated by prohibited earnings or acquired through prohibited expenditure (para 15).

Disclose asset risk concentrations by economic sector, by customer (without naming), by domestic geographic area, and by each foreign country (para 16); disclose net foreign-currency asset/liability risk by currency type (para 17).

Disclose material amounts recoverable from reinsurers or other parties (para 18); material contingencies not recognized in the statement of financial position (para 19); and outstanding material financial commitments that cannot be cancelled without significant cost or penalty (para 20).

Disclose significant subsequent events that could materially affect financial position or results of operations (para 21); disclose restricted assets or assets mortgaged/pledged as security (para 22).

Accounting policy changes require description, justification, and effect on policyholders' surplus/deficit, net income, and prior-period retained earnings (para 23); accounting estimate changes require description and effect on current/future period results (para 24); correction of material prior-period errors requires nature and effect on policyholders'/owners' equity for prior and current periods (para 25).

Disclose the party managing insurance operations and the consideration it receives (para 26); the party investing policyholders' and owners' equity funds and the bases for allocating investment profit (para 27); and the basis for allocating insurance operations surplus and investment profits among policyholders (para 28).

Related parties defined (para 29) as: board members/general manager and deputies; their relatives to the second degree with vested financial interest; significant voting-unit owners and their relatives; entities commonly controlled; subsidiaries and affiliates; entities the company can influence via ownership. Disclosure of related-party transactions must include relationship nature, transaction terms/amounts (including total claims paid and contribution rate offered), and period-end balances due (para 30).

Disclose material transactions with external auditors and/or members of the Shari'a supervisory board (para 31); disclose concentration of insurance and reinsurance risk by geographic area, economic sector, and reinsurer (para 32).

Statement of financial position: assets/liabilities not set off absent a Shar'i, legal right or practice requirement (para 35); items grouped by nature and presented in order of relative liquidity, with no current/noncurrent classification (para 38); asset line items include cash and cash equivalents, contributions receivable, reinsurance receivables, deferred sales receivables (Murabaha, Salam, Istisna'a), investment securities, Mudaraba financing, Musharaka financing, investments in other entities' capital, real estate, leased assets, fixed assets (para 39); liability line items include unearned contributions, outstanding claims, claims incurred but not reported, Zakah and taxes payable (para 40); policyholders' equity shown as a separate item between liabilities and owners' equity (para 41); minority interest in consolidated statements shown separately between policyholders' equity and owners' equity (para 42).

Statement of policyholders' revenues and expenses discloses gross contributions, reinsurance share, changes in unearned contributions, earned contributions, claims paid and outstanding, acquisition cost, investment income, managing-party remuneration, and technical surplus/deficit (paras 44-47); income statement discloses investment revenue/expense/gains/losses by type, revaluation gains/losses, Zakah and taxes separately, net income, and the Zakah base wherever the company is obligated to pay Zakah (paras 48-53); minority interest shown as a separate item before net income in the consolidated income statement (para 54).

Statement of cash flows differentiates operating, investing, and financing activities and discloses net cash change plus non-cash transactions (paras 55-58); statement of changes in owners' equity discloses paid-in capital, reserves, retained earnings, capital contributions, net income, and distributions (paras 59-60); statement of policyholders' surplus (or deficit) discloses opening balance, period surplus/deficit, distributions, and closing balance (paras 61-62); statement of sources and uses of funds in the Zakah and charity fund discloses the company's responsibility for Zakah payment on behalf of owners/policyholders and fund disbursements (paras 63-66).
Effective date: this Standard is effective for financial statements for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1421 A.H. or 1 January 2000 A.D. (para 79).

key_points: Standard applies to Shari'a-compliant funds financially independent of their establishing institution; excludes funds shown on the establishing institution's own statement of financial position and restricted investment-account funds not in share/unit form (para 1).

Complete set of Fund financial statements: Statement of Net Assets, Statement of Portfolio Investments/Receivables/Financing, Statement of Operations, Statement of Changes in Net Assets or Cash Flow, Statement of Financial Highlights, Notes, and the Shari'a Supervisory Board report (para 2).
Comparative financial statements are required and must let users distinguish actual changes from accounting-policy changes (para 3).
Form, classification and terminology used must ensure clear, understandable presentation of financial statement content (para 4).
Pages and notes must be numbered consecutively and cross-referenced to the related financial statement items (para 5).
Notes are an integral part of the financial statements; every page must carry the notes-range statement (para 6).
Statement of Net Assets covers all assets/liabilities at period end by main classification, with Fund shares/units and net asset value per share/unit shown at the bottom (para 7).
Net asset value per share/unit is calculated by dividing net assets by the number of outstanding shares/units (para 9).
Assets reported consecutively as: cash and cash equivalents; investments (income/trading); receivables (e.g. Murabaha, Salam, Istisna'a receivables); financing; other assets (para 10).
Investments measured at cash equivalent value, or net book value if unavailable, with gross book value and valuation provisions disclosed (para 12).
Receivables measured at cash equivalent value = historical cost less provision for doubtful debts and deferred income (para 14).
Financing measured at cash equivalent value, or net book value if unavailable, with gross value and provisions disclosed (para 16).
Liabilities reported, if material, as accounts payable, accrued liabilities, and other liabilities (para 20).
Statement of Portfolio Investments, Receivables and Financing discloses each asset type as a percentage of total assets, indicating adherence to investment objectives (para 22).

Statement of Operations sections: income from investments/sales/financing; expenses; net income/loss; realized and/or unrealized gains/losses; net gains/losses; net income before the Mudarib share; increase/decrease in net assets after the Mudarib share (para 25).

Expenses include management fees (agency-managed Funds), professional fees, administrative expenses, registration fees, marketing expenses, and other expenses; material items reported separately (para 27).
Cash dividend income recognized at the declared amount payable in cash on the date of declaration (para 31).
Realized capital gains/losses recognized at sale date, measured as sale price less carrying amount plus disposal-related expenses (para 33).
Statement of Changes in Net Assets is preferable when investments are mostly highly liquid, carried at market value, and the liability-to-total-assets ratio is low (para 37).

Statement of Changes in Net Assets comprises: increase/decrease from operations, distributions to shareholders/unitholders, share/unit transactions, capital contributions, and net change in net assets (para 39).

Statement of Financial Highlights covers the three most recent financial periods per share/unit, including NAV, income before/after Mudarib share, distributions, and capital contributions (paras 45-46).

Notes disclosures required include: Fund type/activities/policies (para 48); redemption bases (para 52); manager and custodian contractual relationships (para 53); related-party transactions per FAS No. (1) (para 57); Mudarib share or agent's fee (para 58); Shari'a-prohibited earnings and their disposal (para 61); whether Zakah is the Fund's or shareholders'/unitholders' responsibility, plus Zakah due per share/unit (para 62); tax provisioning (para 63); Fund duration and liquidation conditions (para 64).

Real estate assets measured at historical cost plus direct ownership expenses on acquisition, then revalued to cash equivalent value using the latest real estate valuer's valuation (or historical cost if unavailable) (paras 65-66).

standards.structure: 1. Scope of the Standard (para 1). 2. Technical Provisions: 2/1 Types of technical provisions (paras 2-4); 2/2 Recognition of technical provisions (para 5); 2/3 Measurement of technical provisions (paras 6-8); 2/4 Presentation requirements (paras 9-10); 2/5 Disclosure in the notes to the financial statements (paras 11-13). 3. Reserves: 3/1 Types of reserves (paras 14-15); 3/2 Recognition of reserves (para 16); 3/3 Measurement of reserves (para 17); 3/4 Presentation requirements (paras 18-19); 3/5 Disclosure in the notes to the financial statements (paras 20-22). 4. Effective Date (para 23). Adoption of the Standard. Appendix (A): Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard. key_points: Standard applies to main technical provisions established by companies for general insurance (property and casualty) operations (para 1).
Standard also applies to the deficit reserve and equalisation reserve set aside by the company from surplus before allocation to policyholders (para 1).
Standard does not apply to reserves within owners' equity set aside from earnings to meet legal or general requirements, nor to the depreciation provision (para 1).
Any conflict between the standard's requirements and the company's charter or the laws/regulations of its operating country must be disclosed (para 1).
Three types of technical provisions for general insurance: unearned contributions provision, outstanding claims, and claims incurred but not reported (paras 2-4).
Unearned contributions provision is an amount set aside to meet claims related to unearned contributions which may arise in the current or future financial periods (para 2).
Outstanding claims provision is an amount set aside for claims expected to be paid that were incurred and reported up to period end, including claims handling expenses less settled claims (para 3).
Claims incurred but not reported (IBNR) provision covers claims that were incurred but not reported until after the end of the current financial period (para 4).
All technical provisions are recognised when set up at the end of the financial period and recorded as an expense in the 'Statement of Policyholders' Revenue and Expenses' (para 5).

Unearned contributions provision is measured as a percentage of total unearned contributions, after deducting the reinsurance share, using one of four methods: (a) 40% non-marine/25% marine or another percentage, (b) the 24-month method, (c) the 360-day method, (d) any other method; the method used must be disclosed (para 6).

Outstanding claims provision is measured as the amount of outstanding claims estimated by the company, sufficient to cover claims incurred and reported to period end, after deducting reinsurance share and settled claims (para 7).
Claims incurred but not reported provision is measured as the amount estimated by the company based on past experience of recent reported claims and various statistical methods (para 8).
All technical provisions are presented separately, at period end, under 'technical provisions' on the liabilities side of the statement of financial position (para 9).
The amount expected to be recovered from reinsurance, related to all technical provisions, is presented on the assets side under 'amount expected to be recovered from reinsurance' (para 10).
Company must disclose, for each type of technical provision and each insurance business type, the opening balance, amounts added, amounts used, and closing balance for the period (para 11).
Company must disclose the basis applied in determining each type of technical provision, and any changes made to that basis (para 12).
Disclosure requirements of Financial Accounting Standard No. (12), General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Insurance Companies, should also be observed (para 13).

Two types of reserves: deficit reserve, a cushion against future deficit (para 14), and equalization reserve, to mitigate the effect of exceptionally high loss ratios for classes of insurance with high claims volatility (para 15).
Deficit reserve and equalization reserve are recognised when the company's management decides to set up these reserves (para 16).

Reserves are measured at the amount deemed prudent by management; a shortfall to the required level is treated as an appropriation of surplus, and any excess over the prudent amount is deducted from reserves and added back to policyholders' surplus for the period (para 17).

Deficit reserve is presented separately under policyholders' equity in the statement of financial position (para 18); equalization reserve is likewise presented separately under policyholders' equity (para 19).

Company must disclose the bases applied in determining and measuring both reserves (para 20), the changes occurring in each reserve during the period, including opening balance, amounts added and used, and closing balance (para 21), and the party that will receive remaining reserve balances in case of liquidation (para 22).
Standard is effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1423 A.H. or 1 January 2002 A.D. (para 23).

standards.applicability: Applies to Islamic banks and financial institutions (defined in Preface fn. 1) for recognizing, measuring, presenting and disclosing transactions in currencies other than the reporting currency (assets, liabilities, off-balance sheet items, revenues, expenses, gains or losses), and covers net investments in foreign operations such as branches and subsidiaries preparing statements in a different currency, and foreign currency items in the statement of changes in restricted investments; where the Standard conflicts with the Islamic bank's charter or the laws/regulations of the country of operation, that conflict must be disclosed (para. 1).
standards.structure: 1. Scope of the Standard (para. 1). 2. Accounting Treatment for Foreign Currency Transactions: 2/1 non-Mudaraba/Musharaka transactions (para. 2); 2/2 Mudaraba/Musharaka transactions (paras. 3-6); 2/3 foreign-currency Murabaha to the Purchase Orderer with grace period (para. 7); 2/4 client settlement of Murabaha receivable (paras. 8-9); 2/5 Murabaha converted to Musawama (para. 10). 3. Accounting Treatment for the Purpose of Preparing Financial Statements: 3/1 monetary assets/liabilities translation (para. 11); 3/2 net investment in foreign operation translation differences (para. 12); 3/3 accumulated unrealised gains (para. 13); 3/4 severe devaluation losses (para. 14); 3/5 settlement in another currency (para. 15); 3/6 revenues/expenses translation (para. 16); 3/7 Zakah (para. 17). 4. Presentation Requirements: 4/1 unrestricted investment account FX differences (para. 18); 4/2 owners' equity FX differences (para. 19); 4/3 disposal of foreign operation (para. 20). 5. Disclosure in the Notes to the Financial Statements: 5/1-5/8 (paras. 21-28). 6. Effective Date (para. 29). Adoption of the Standard. Appendix (A): Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard. Appendix (B): Juristic Rules for Foreign Currency Transactions and Foreign Operations. Appendix (C): Reasons for the Standard. Appendix (D): Basis for Conclusions. Appendix (E): Definitions.
key_points: The term 'Islamic bank' or 'Islamic banks' used throughout the Standard refers to Islamic banks and financial institutions undertaking foreign currency transactions and foreign operations (fn 1).

The Standard sets out rules for recognizing, measuring, presenting and disclosing transactions in currencies other than the reporting currency, covers net investments in foreign operations (branches/subsidiaries reporting in a different currency), applies to restricted investment account statements, and requires disclosure of any conflict with the bank's charter or local laws/regulations (para. 1).

Foreign currency transactions not based on Mudaraba or Musharaka contracts are recognised on the transaction date by translating them into the reporting currency at the prevailing spot exchange rate (para. 2).

Mudaraba/Musharaka foreign currency transactions are recognised by translating amounts into the reporting currency at the prevailing spot exchange rate on the date of receipt of the foreign currency (para. 3).
If the Mudaraba/Musharaka transaction is executed in the reporting currency, the capital shall be remitted -- after addition of profits or deduction of losses -- in the reporting currency (para. 4).

If executed in a currency other than the reporting currency, gain or loss is determined by retranslating Mudaraba/Musharaka assets into the reporting currency, credited or charged against the Mudaraba/Musharaka fund (para. 5).

If the provider of funds asks the Islamic bank to retranslate the due amount back to the currency in which the capital was originally received, any resultant translation gain or loss is credited/charged to the client (para. 6).

A foreign-currency Murabaha to the Purchase Orderer transaction with a grace period from the supplier is measured by translating the foreign-currency amount committed to the supplier at the prevailing spot exchange rate at the time the transaction was concluded with the supplier (para. 7).

If the client settles the Murabaha receivable in the currency in which the transaction was executed, the resulting profit of the transaction shall initially be recognised in that currency and translated into the reporting currency at the prevailing spot exchange rate on the settlement date (para. 8).

If the client settles the Murabaha receivable in a currency other than that of the transaction, the amount paid is translated into the reporting currency at the prevailing spot exchange rate on the settlement date, and any resulting foreign exchange gain or loss is the responsibility of the Islamic bank (para. 9).

If a Murabaha with a grace period is cancelled and re-executed as Musawama with deferred settlement, the client's settlement amount is translated into the reporting currency at the prevailing spot exchange rate on the settlement date, and any resultant gain or loss is recognised in the Islamic bank's income statement (para. 10).

Monetary assets and liabilities denominated in foreign currencies are translated at the prevailing spot exchange rates at the date of the financial statements; translation differences other than those from net investments in foreign operations are recognised in the income statement (para. 11).

Foreign exchange differences from retranslating a net investment in a foreign operation are recognised as a separate component of equity in the statement of financial position, split between owners' equity and unrestricted investment accountholders' equity; on disposal, the differences are recognised as a gain or loss in the income statement (para. 12).

Accumulated unrealised gains from retranslating a net investment in a foreign operation are first credited against any accumulated unrealised losses of prior years charged to the separate equity component; a resulting accumulated gain represents an increase in the carrying amount of the net investment (para. 13).

Translation losses from severe (non-temporary) devaluation or depreciation of the currency of a net investment in a foreign operation are first charged against any credit balance on the separate equity component, with any remainder recognised as a loss in the income statement (para. 14).

If receivables or liabilities denominated in a foreign currency are settled fully or partially in another currency, the amount settled is measured at the prevailing spot exchange rate on the settlement date, with any translation difference recognised as a currency exchange gain or loss in the income statement (para. 15).

At the date of the financial statements, all revenues and expenses of the Islamic bank's foreign operations are translated into the reporting currency using the weighted average method or an acceptable approximation (para. 16).

Zakah is calculated based on Financial Accounting Standard No. (9): Zakah, at period end, after translating all monetary foreign-currency assets and liabilities into the reporting currency at the prevailing spot exchange rates at the end of the financial period (para. 17).

Foreign exchange differences attributable to unrestricted investment accounts are presented in the income statement under 'gain or loss on foreign currency transactions for unrestricted investment accounts,' after 'return on unrestricted investment accounts' and before deducting the Islamic bank's share as mudarib (para. 18).

Gains or losses from revaluation of foreign-currency monetary assets/liabilities attributable to owners' equity are presented under 'gain or loss on foreign currency translation' before 'other revenues,' excluding gains/losses on net investments in foreign operations (para. 19).

On disposal of a foreign operation, any gain or loss on retranslation of the net investment is presented separately under 'gain or loss on foreign currency translation'; prior-period unrealised amounts previously in the separate equity component are recognised in the income statement in the period of disposal (para. 20).

Disclosure requirements: reason for using a reporting currency different from the local currency (para. 21); nature, reason and effect of an important change in the classification of foreign operations, with possible exemption in the first implementation year (para. 22); separate disclosure of accumulated unrealised gains and losses on net investments, labeled 'Cumulative unrealised translation gains (losses) on net investment in foreign operations' (para. 23); disclosure of differences from translating Mudaraba/Musharaka transactions held in foreign currencies (para. 24).

Further disclosure requirements: material differences, gain or loss, from retranslating unrestricted investment accounts (para. 25); foreign exchange differences on restricted investment accounts, disclosed in the statement of changes in restricted investment accounts (para. 26); policies applied by the Islamic bank in translating foreign currencies and in managing foreign currency risk (para. 27); disclosure requirements of Financial Accounting Standard No. (1) must also be observed (para. 28).
The Standard is effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1423 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 2002 A.D. (para. 29).

divergence_evidence.position: AAOIFI: currency translation (revaluation) is an accounting procedure distinct from a currency-exchange contract and must use the prevailing spot exchange rate on the relevant date; it is not permissible for any reason to use a future or forward exchange rate to translate an obligation, since this would amount to an unauthorized future currency exchange without set-off; exchanging the currency of an unsettled liability (rescheduling) without simultaneous settlement is Riba and prohibited, but where currency translation coincides exactly with settlement of the liability this constitutes a mutual set-off of liabilities, and possession through set-off is tantamount to actual (constructive) possession, discharging the parties -- a ruling confirmed by International Islamic Fiqh Academy Resolution No. (75) 6/8 (Appendix B).
clauses: 'The translation (revaluation) of one currency to another does not refer to a currency exchange transaction involving two currencies, either a spot transaction or a deferred or forward transaction. Instead, translation is an accounting procedure' (Appendix B)

'it is not permissible for whatever reason to carry out the translation process using a future or forward exchange rate, as this would involve translating an obligation that will be settled in the future' (Appendix B)
'this would mean the rescheduling of the liability, potentially involving a change in the effective amount to be paid in lieu of time, which is Riba that is prohibited by Shari'a' (Appendix B)

'if the translation from one currency to another takes place at the same time of the settlement of an obligation, then this is considered as a mutual set-off of liabilities. As a principle, possession through set-off is tantamount to actual possession... the process becomes a currency exchange by virtue of constructive possession that discharges the parties from liability' -- confirmed by International Islamic Fiqh Academy Resolution No. (75) 6/8 (Appendix B, fn 4, fn 5)
'It is imperative that the transaction be recorded at the prevailing spot exchange rate on the date of execution' (Appendix B)

'there is no justification for using a future exchange rate as a basis for the currency translation because this involves speculation as no one knows what the future rate will be. Hence, the use of spot exchange rates prevails' (Appendix B)

standards.applicability: Applies to institutions which offer Islamic financial services in addition to their conventional financial services; the standard sets out accounting rules only for the Islamic financial services offered by these institutions, not their conventional business (para. 1). 'Institution/institutions' are defined as financial institutions which do not comply with Shari'a rules and principles in all of their transactions (fn. 1).
standards.structure: Preface (objective and disclosure purpose). Statement of the Standard (paras 1-17): 1. Scope of the Standard (para 1); 2. General Provisions — four organizational arrangements 2/1-2/4 (para 2); 3. Appendix (A): Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard. Appendix (B): Reasons for the Standard. Appendix (C): Basis for Conclusions.
key_points: Standard sets out accounting rules for recognizing, measuring and presenting assets managed and funds mobilized on the basis of Shari'a rules and principles by conventional financial institutions offering Islamic financial services, plus related income and disclosures (Preface).
'Institution/institutions' means financial institutions which do not comply with Shari'a rules and principles in all of their transactions (fn. 1).
Scope limited to institutions offering Islamic financial services alongside conventional services; sets accounting rules only for the Islamic financial services portion (para 1).

Four organizational/administrative arrangements recognized: branches with separate or non-separate accounts from conventional branches (2/1); Islamic investment funds (2/2); separate or non-separate Islamic financial services units (2/3); existing conventional units with no separation between the two practices (2/4) (para 2).

Institutions offering services through branches with separate accounts must group those branches for financial reporting and prepare a consolidated supplementary set of financial statements based on AAOIFI standards, published as an appendix to the notes to the financial statements (para 3).
Institutions managing Islamic investment funds shall apply AAOIFI accounting standards, particularly Financial Accounting Standard No. (14): Investment Funds (para 4).

Institutions with separate or non-separate accounts for Islamic services (via conventional departments or separate Islamic units) shall apply AAOIFI income recognition and measurement rules, with detailed disclosure of these rules in the notes (para 5).

Such institutions shall prepare a separate supplementary statement, published in the notes, showing in detail the funds mobilized according to Shari'a rules and principles and the assets financed by these funds (para 6).

Such institutions shall prepare a separate supplementary statement, published in the notes, showing in detail the income and expenses (including provisions) related to Islamic financial services offered (para 7).

Institutions shall disclose accounting policies used for recognition, measurement and presentation of Islamic-service assets/liabilities that are not in accordance with or specified in AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards, plus the nature of such assets and liabilities (para 8).

Institutions declaring Shari'a compliance must appoint a Shari'a supervisory board which presents a Shari'a report, and must implement the Governance Standards issued by AAOIFI relating to that board (para 9).

Exceptional case of no Shari'a Supervisory Board (requires regulatory/supervisory approval): institution must disclose reasons for not appointing a board, how Shari'a compliance is achieved in the services offered, and which body approves those services (para 10).
Institutions shall disclose whether or not they commingle funds relating to Islamic financial services with funds relating to conventional financial services (para 11).

Institutions shall disclose in detail the sources and applications of funds mobilized and invested by their Islamic financial services, and the sources of funds used to cover a deficit if one occurs (para 12).

Institutions shall disclose any revenues or expenditures prohibited by Shari'a rules and principles related to Shari'a-mobilized funds, and the disposition of such revenues as determined by the Shari'a supervisory board (para 13).
Institutions shall disclose any reserves deducted from Shari'a-mobilized funds, the purposes of such reserves, and to whom the reserves revert if the related activities have ceased (para 14).
Institutions shall disclose the percentage amount of funds relating to Islamic financial services compared to the percentage amount of funds relating to conventional financial services (para 15).

Disclosure requirements stated in Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions should also be observed (para 16).
Effective date: financial periods beginning 1 Muharram, 1424 A.H., or 1 January, 2003 A.D. (para 17).
Standard adopted by the AAOIFI Accounting and Auditing Standards Board at meeting No. (23) held on 17 Safar, 1423 A.H., corresponding to 30 April, 2002 A.D. (Adoption of the Standard).
A study sample of five institutions found the percentage of Islamic funds compared to total assets of these institutions ranged between 20% and 40% (Appendix B).

Study found these institutions had no Shari'a supervisory board of their own, instead relying on Shari'a rulings of other Islamic financial institutions' boards, and did not disclose the Shari'a rules they followed (Appendix B).

Basis for Conclusions ties the standard's disclosure and recognition requirements to the previous Statement of Financial Accounting No. (1): Objectives, and the previous Statement of Financial Accounting No. (2): Concepts, for Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions (Appendix C).

Appendix A traces the standard's drafting history: priority given at Board meeting No. (16), 8-9 Ramadan 1419 A.H./26-27 December 1998; consultant commissioned 1 Ramadan 1421 A.H./27 November 2000; reviewed at Accounting Standards Committee meetings No. (27)-(30) and Shari'a Committee meeting No. (6) through 2001; a listening session held in Bahrain on 22 Dhul-Qa'dah 1422 A.H./4 February 2002 with more than 20 participants; adopted at Board meeting No. (23) (Appendix A).
divergence_notes: "there are differences in the Shari'a rules used by these institutions and that they have no Shari'a supervisory board" — noted among conventional institutions offering Islamic financial services, who instead rely on rulings of other Islamic institutions' Shari'a boards (Appendix B).

key_points: Standard applies to contributions made on a donation basis by policyholders relating to general insurance, and to the donation-based portion of Takaful contributions for insurance on persons (para 1).
Standard excludes the investment/saving portion of contributions in insurance on persons (para 1).
Any conflict between the standard and the company's charter or the laws/regulations of its country of operation must be disclosed (para 1).
Earned contributions are recognized as a separate item 'Earned contributions' in the Statement of Policyholders' Revenue and Expenses at inception of the policy or of the insured risk (para 2).
Where contributions are undertaken through intermediaries, the intermediaries' commission is recognized separately as an expense in the Statement of Policyholders' Revenue and Expenses (para 2).

Unearned contributions relating to subsequent financial periods are recognized as a liability item 'Unearned contributions' in the Statement of Financial Position, at inception of the policy or insured risk (para 3).
Contributions due to be received at period-end are recognized on the assets side of the Statement of Financial Position under 'Contributions receivable' as an item of policyholders' equity (para 4).

At period-end the company must estimate changes in contributions for policy types subject to change; increases are recognized once receipt is assured, decreases are recognized once the decrease is assured (para 5).
Estimated changes in contributions and their effect on the original contributions must reflect the risks attached, and be considered when determining earned/unearned portions at period-end (para 5).

The reinsurance share of earned contributions is recognized as an expense 'Reinsurance share' in the Statement of Policyholders' Revenue and Expenses at inception of the policy or insured risk (para 6).
Reinsurance commission due to the company from Islamic reinsurance companies is recognized as revenue 'Reinsurance commissions' at the inception of the reinsurance contract (para 7).

Contributions are measured at period-end at the amount determined by the company, estimated by the company's actuaries using actuarial techniques and statistical methods, plus international prevailing practices and home-country regulations (para 8).

Contributions undertaken through intermediaries are measured at the amount underwritten by the intermediary, either the gross amount or the net amount after commission deduction, depending on the transfer obligation (para 8).

Earned contributions presented in the Statement of Policyholders' Revenue and Expenses must be net of: reinsurance share; change in contributions from policies initiated in prior periods; change in unearned contributions; and intermediary-related contribution changes before period-end (para 9).
Disclosure required of accounting policies for treatment of contributions from both general insurance and insurance on individuals (para 10).
Disclosure required of accounting policies for treatment of any changes occurring in contributions during the financial period (para 11).
Disclosure required of accounting policy for policyholder withdrawal with no eligibility for any part of the contribution (para 12).
Disclosure required of accounting policy for policyholder withdrawal with eligibility for part of the contribution based on remaining policy period (para 12).
Disclosure required of accounting policy for cancellation of the policy and its effect on policyholder eligibility for part or whole of the contribution, and any other applicable method (para 12).
Separate disclosure required of contribution receivables relating to policyholders, other insurance companies, and reinsurance companies (para 13).
Disclosure required of the breakdown of contributions on the basis of insurance segments and type of insurance (para 14).
General disclosure requirements stated in other AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards related to Islamic insurance companies must also be observed (para 15).
Standard is effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1425 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 2004 A.D. (para 16).
