key_points: Scope: applies to financial statements published by IFIs regardless of legal form, country of incorporation, or size; applies to parent/subsidiary/associate separate statements (consolidated-only when both presented); applies regardless of public/private security status; conflicts with charter/law must be disclosed (para 1).

Operating segment defined as a distinguishable component earning revenue/incurring expense, whose results are regularly reviewed by the chief operating decision maker (board of directors or CEO), and for which discrete financial information is available (para 2).
An operating segment may exist before earning revenues, e.g. start-up operations (para 3).
Business segment and Geographic segment defined as distinguishable components with risks/returns that may differ from other segments in the same category (para 4).
Business segments may be combined into one if substantially similar in the majority of: long-term financial performance, nature of products/services, customer type, distribution method (para 5).
Geographic segments may be combined into one if substantially similar in the majority of: economic/political conditions, relationships between operations, proximity of operations (para 6).
Reportable segment = a business/geographic segment (per para 4), possibly aggregated per para 5 or 6, that exceeds the quantitative thresholds in para 8 (para 7).
Quantitative threshold: reportable segment's revenue is 10% or more of total revenue (para 8).

Quantitative threshold: reportable segment's result (profit or loss) is 10% or more of the combined result of all segments in profit, or of all segments in loss, whichever is greater in absolute amount (para 8).
Quantitative threshold: reportable segment's assets are 10% or more of total assets of all segments (para 8).
Segments not meeting the para 8 thresholds may be combined into a separate reportable segment only if they share a majority of the para 5/6 aggregation criteria (para 9).
Segments not separately reportable are combined and disclosed in an 'Other' category, separate from other reconciling items (para 10).

Specific disclosure: segment revenue and expense per reportable segment, classified per Income Statement headings, with external-customer revenue separated from inter-segment revenue (para 11); segment result disclosed for each reportable segment (para 12).

Specific disclosure: total segment assets and segment liabilities disclosed per Statement of Financial Position headings (para 13); nature and amount of extraordinary segment revenue/expense items disclosed where relevant to explaining performance (para 14).
Specific disclosure: reconciliation between reportable-segment revenue, expense, assets, and liabilities and the institution's/consolidated totals (para 15).

General disclosure: factors used to identify reportable segments and basis of organization (products/services, geography, regulatory environment, or combination); a statement is required if discrete financial information is unavailable (para 16).
General disclosure: types of products and services from which each reportable segment derives its revenues (para 17).
Institutions are encouraged (not required) to disclose the broad operating objectives set for each segment and comment on the extent achieved (para 18).

Reclassification rules: a newly identified segment requires reclassification of prior-period comparative data (para 19); a change in segment composition requires reclassification of earlier-period information (para 20); if reclassification is impracticable, both old and new segmentation bases are reported in the year of change (para 21).

Segment information must be prepared per the accounting policies used for the institution's/consolidated financial statements (para 22); material accounting-policy changes affecting segment reporting must be disclosed (nature, reasons, restatement status, financial effect if determinable), with prior-period data restated unless impracticable (para 23).
Disclosure requirements of Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Financial Institutions must also be observed (para 24).
Effective date: financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1426 A.H. or 1 January 2005 A.D. (para 25).

Juristic basis (Mudaraba): the financier (rabb al-mal) is entitled to assess and supervise the mudarib's activities and ensure contractual limitations are observed, consistent with the principle of non-interference in the mudarib's work (Appendix B).

Juristic basis (agency): the principal is entitled to observe investment operations conducted under an agency appointment, since the agent's remuneration is unaffected by the investment outcome, justifying stakeholder awareness of products and services (Appendix B).

key_points: Standard applies to consolidated financial statements prepared and presented by an IFI as a parent entity, sets principles for determining entities subject to consolidation, and prescribes accounting for investment in subsidiaries by the parent (para 1).

Consolidation also applies to Special Purpose Vehicles (SPV) — entities established to carry out specific activities and accomplish specific objectives — except where the SPV is established for the benefit of a party or parties other than the IFI; conflicts between the standard and an IFI's charter or local laws/regulations must be disclosed (para 1).
'Control' is defined as the power to govern the financial and operating policies of an entity with the objective of obtaining benefits from its operations (para 2).

'Subsidiary' is defined as an entity controlled by the parent; 'Parent' is the entity that prepares and presents consolidated financial statements, and in this standard the IFI is regarded as the parent; 'Voting rights' are rights for voting at an entity's shareholders' meeting or other similar forums (para 2).
Control is presumed to exist where an IFI holds, directly or indirectly through its subsidiaries, more than 50% of the voting rights in an entity, unless clearly demonstrated otherwise (para 3).

Where the IFI has less than majority voting rights, control may still exist through: (I) agreement with the entity's other shareholders or the entity itself; (II) rights arising from other contractual arrangements; (III) the IFI's de facto power via its voting rights; (IV) potential voting rights; or (V) a combination thereof (para 3).

Control attributable to investments funded by (a) the IFI's owners' equity and liabilities and (b) its unrestricted investment accounts must be considered in determining a subsidiary and requires consolidation by the IFI (para 4).

Only substantive voting rights are considered in assessing whether the IFI has power over an entity; rights must be exercisable when relevant decisions are required and the holder must have the practical ability to exercise them; determination of voting rights includes current substantive voting rights and currently-exercisable voting rights (para 5).
Consolidation of a subsidiary is required regardless of the nature of its activities, including where dissimilar to those of the IFI (para 6).
The IFI ceases to account for investment in a subsidiary once it is no longer able to exercise control; the investment is then accounted for as an associate or investment, as appropriate (para 7).

An IFI is required to prepare and present consolidated financial statements combining its own separate statements with those of its subsidiaries (para 8); it may also present separate financial statements not consolidating subsidiaries, per local regulation or its own volition (para 9), but such separate statements must be accompanied by the consolidated financial statements (para 10).
Consolidated statements are prepared by combining like items line by line, except that line-by-line combination is not required where control is intended to be temporary (para 11).
Intragroup transactions between the IFI and subsidiaries are eliminated; intragroup losses may indicate impairment requiring recognition in the consolidated financial statements (para 12).
The carrying amount of the IFI's investment in subsidiaries and its portion of equity in those entities is eliminated, with resultant goodwill (para 13).

Non-controlling interests in the statement of financial position must be identified and reported as part of total equity; net profit or loss attributable to non-controlling interest must be disclosed separately from that attributable to the parent (para 14).
The same accounting policy must be applied to the parent's, subsidiary's, and consolidated financial statements (para 15).

Financial statements subject to consolidation must be prepared as at the same reporting date and for the same reporting period; if not practicable, the difference between subsidiary and parent reporting dates must be no more than three months, with significant intervening transactions adjusted in the consolidated statements (para 16).

Subsidiary income and expenses are consolidated from the date of acquisition; on full or partial disposal, the difference between the carrying amount of the investment and disposal proceeds is recognised in the income statement, corresponding goodwill is derecognised proportionately, and consolidation continues until the date control ceases (paras 17-18).

Foreign currency transactions and foreign operations in the consolidated financial statements must follow Financial Accounting Standard No. (16): Foreign Currency Transactions and Foreign Operations (para 19).

If a parent ceases to classify a subsidiary's control as temporary, the subsidiary's financial statements are consolidated on a line-by-line basis for all periods presented, with prior-period amounts restated (para 20).

Disclosures required: a list of subsidiaries with names, nature of business, country of incorporation, shareholding, level of voting rights, and basis of control (para 21); a list of entities where the IFI will potentially hold more than 50% of voting rights in future via not-yet-exercisable voting rights, with details and the date those rights become exercisable (para 22); significant restrictions on financial/commercial transactions or shareholding relationships among subsidiaries and the IFI (para 23); details of entities where control is intended to be temporary (para 24); and separate identification of non-controlling interests funded by restricted investment accounts, disclosed as 'Non-controlling Interests – Restricted Investment Account' in the notes (para 25).
This Standard is effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1431 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 2010 A.D. (para 26).

The revised Standard was adopted by the Accounting and Auditing Standards Board at meeting No. (35) on 6 Rabi' II 1430 A.H., corresponding to 2 April 2009 A.D.; the original Standard on Consolidation was approved at meeting No. (32) on 22 Rabi' II 1428 A.H., corresponding to 9 May 2007 A.D., with the review decided at meeting No. (33) on 29 May 2008 A.D. alongside development of a new Standard on Investments in Associates (Adoption of the Standard; Appendix A).

Under the revised Standard it is not mandatory for an IFI to hold more than 50% of shares of the subsidiary to demonstrate control; an IFI holding less than majority voting rights may have de facto power where it holds significantly dominant voting rights giving it practical ability to unilaterally direct financial and operating policies (e.g., a large voting block with the remainder widely dispersed and historical shareholder-meeting attendance/voting patterns showing the IFI holds the majority); temporary control is construed as the parent's intention to dispose of the entity within twelve months from acquisition with management actively seeking a buyer (Appendix C).

Disclosure Requirements (22-31); 6. Effective Date (32). Adoption of the Standard. Appendix (A) Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard. Appendix (B) Reasons for the Standard. key_points: Standard applies to financial statements of an IFI; does not apply to investments made by venture capital entities, mutual funds, and similar entities; conflicts with an IFI's charter or local laws/regulations must be disclosed (para 1).
"Associate" is defined as an entity in which the IFI has significant influence (para 2).
"Significant influence" is defined as the capacity of an entity to substantially affect (but not control) the financial and operating policies of another entity (para 2).

"Voting rights" defined as rights for voting at an entity's shareholders' meeting or other similar forums; "Consolidated financial statements" and "Separate financial statements" also defined (para 2).

Significant influence is presumed to exist where an IFI holds, directly or indirectly through its subsidiaries, 20% or more of the voting rights in an entity, unless clearly demonstrated otherwise (para 3).
Significant influence may also exist below the 20% threshold, through an agreement with the entity's other shareholders or the entity itself, regardless of the IFI's level of shareholding (para 3).

Significant influence attributable to investments funded by (a) the IFI's owners' equity and liabilities, or (b) unrestricted investment accounts, is considered for determination of an associate (para 4).

Voting rights include those accorded through shares, other equity or financing instruments, and those obtained through agreement with the entity's other shareholders or the entity itself; determination includes current and currently-exercisable voting rights (para 5).

Investment in an associate is initially recognized when made, under the heading "Investment in Associates"; an investment not initially so classified is included under that heading once it subsequently meets the criteria (paras 6-7).
Initial measurement of the investment in an associate is at cost (para 8).

Subsequent measurement is at carrying amount, adjusted to include the IFI's share of the associate's profit or loss after the investment date; the share of profit or loss is based solely on shareholding, not on voting rights (paras 9-10).

Carrying amount is adjusted for changes in the IFI's proportionate interest arising from unrecognized equity changes in the associate (e.g. asset revaluation) (para 11), and is decreased for dividends or other distributions received (para 12).
Profit or loss from transactions between the IFI and the associate is eliminated from the IFI's share; intragroup losses indicating impairment are recognized in the financial statements (para 13).

Where the IFI's share of loss exceeds the carrying amount of its investment plus any long-term participation, further loss recognition is discontinued; a liability is recognized only to the extent of the IFI's legal obligation or payments made on the associate's behalf; subsequent profit is recognized only after that liability is fully offset (para 14).

The IFI's share of the associate's profit or loss is recognized in the consolidated financial statements as at the reporting date, based on the associate's latest available financial statements (para 15).

The associate should report as at the same date as the IFI; if impracticable, the gap must not exceed three months, with adjustment for the effect of significant transactions occurring between the two reporting dates (para 16).

The same accounting policy should be applied to the associate's and the IFI's financial statements; if the associate uses a different policy, adjustments are made in the associate's separate financial statements (para 17).
The IFI ceases to account for the investment as an associate once it can no longer exercise significant influence (para 18).

Associates acquired with the intention of disposal within twelve months are accounted for at cost less impairment; if not disposed of within twelve months, the investment is accounted for retrospectively per paras 4/3/1 to 4/3/6 (para 19).
The IFI must determine impairment in the value of its investment in an associate at each reporting date and recognize any impairment loss in the statement of income (para 20).
In separate financial statements, investment in associates is accounted for either at cost or fair value (para 21).

Required disclosures include: list of associates (names, business activity, country of incorporation, IFI's shareholding and voting rights) (para 22); reasons for presumed significant influence where the IFI holds less than 20% of an associate's shares (para 23); summary financial information of associates - total assets, liabilities, revenues and profit or loss (para 24); significant restrictions on financial/commercial transactions or shareholding relationships between associates and the IFI (para 25); fair value of investments in associates with published price quotations (para 26); IFI's contingent liabilities arising from associates' liabilities (para 27) and IFI's share of associates' contingent liabilities (para 29); reasons dissimilar accounting policies could not be adjusted (para 30); and unrecognized share of associate losses, for the period and cumulatively (para 31).
Standard is effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1431 A.H. or 1 January 2010 A.D.; earlier adoption is encouraged (para 32).

key_points: Standard applies to an entity's investment whether direct, through structured products, investment funds/portfolios, Sukuk, other debt-type instruments, or shares (para 1).

Standard excludes own equity instruments, investments requiring special treatment (subsidiaries/associates), real estate, insurance contracts with discretionary participation features, and contracts covered by FAS No. (3), (4), (7) and (10) (para 2).
Conflicts between the standard and the entity's charter or local laws/regulations must be disclosed (para 3).
Each investment is segregated as a debt-type instrument or an equity-type instrument (para 4).
Debt-type instruments are investments with terms providing fixed or determinable payments of profits and capital to the holder (para 5).
Equity-type instruments do not exhibit debt-type features and evidence a residual interest in the entity's assets after deducting liabilities (para 6).
Debt-type instruments are classified as: investment at fair value through income statement, or investments carried at amortised cost (para 7).
Equity-type instruments are classified as: investments at fair value through income statement, or investments at fair value through equity (para 8).

An investment is classified 'held for trading' if acquired/originated principally to generate profit from short-term price fluctuations or dealer's margin, including portfolios with an actual pattern of short-term profit taking (para 10).
Designation at fair value through income statement is permitted only if it eliminates an accounting mismatch, or the investment is managed and evaluated internally on a fair value basis (para 11).
A debt-type investment is measured at amortised cost only if managed on a contractual yield basis and not designated at fair value through income statement (para 12).
All investments are initially recognised at fair value plus transaction costs, except fair-value-through-income-statement investments, whose transaction costs are expensed when incurred (para 16).
Amortised cost investments are re-measured each reporting period using the effective profit rate method; amortisation, derecognition and impairment gains/losses go to the income statement (para 17).

Amortised cost investments are tested for impairment each period; impairment is recognised when carrying value exceeds expected recoverable amount, with recoveries recognised through the income statement up to previously recognised losses (para 18).

Investments held for trading and designated at fair value through income statement are re-measured to fair value each period with gain/loss split between owners' equity and investment accountholders (paras 19-20).

Investments designated at fair value through equity are re-measured to fair value, with gain/loss recognised in the 'Investments fair value reserve' in equity, split between owners' and investment accountholders' equity (para 21).
Where fair value of equity instruments cannot be reliably determined on a continuing basis, they are measured at cost until a reliable fair value becomes determinable (para 22).
A significant or prolonged decline in fair value of an equity instrument below its cost is objective evidence of impairment for fair-value-through-equity investments (para 23).

Realised gains/losses on sale are measured as the difference between carrying amount and net cash proceeds (or maturity value for debt-type instruments), recognised in the income statement with the owners'/investment-accountholder split (para 26).

No reclassification into or out of the fair value and amortised cost categories (debt-type) or fair value through income statement and equity categories (equity-type) is permitted after initial designation (paras 28-29).
Fair value disclosure hierarchy: (a) quoted prices in active markets for identical instruments; (b) directly/indirectly observable inputs; (c) inputs not based on observable market data (para 41).
Effective date: financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1432 A.H. / 1 January 2011 A.D.; earlier application permitted with disclosure of early adoption (para 48).

Standard applied retroactively per FAS No. (1); if retroactive application of the effective profit method or impairment requirements is impracticable, the fair value at the date of initial application becomes the new amortised cost (paras 49, 51).

This revised standard supersedes the previous FAS No. (17) on Investments (first issued 2002 A.D.), which narrowly covered only Sukuk, equity shares and real estate investment (Appendix B; Appendix D).

key_points: Investment in real estate is defined as property held to earn periodical income or for capital appreciation or both, rather than for use in production/supply of goods or services or administrative purposes (owner-occupied) or for sale in the ordinary course of business (inventory) (para 2/4).
Standard applies to the entity's direct investment in real estate acquired for periodical income and/or capital appreciation (para 1/1).
Excludes measurement of real estate leased under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, recognition of lease income, and related disclosures, which are covered by FAS No. (8) (para 1/2).

Real estate held to earn periodical consideration under an operating Ijarah (as defined in FAS No. 8) must nonetheless use one of the two subsequent-measurement methods in this standard, applied consistently in future periods (para 1/2).
Excludes investment in real estate related to agricultural activities and rights/resources related to mining and exploration such as oil and natural gas (para 1/3).
Conflict between the standard and the entity's charter or local laws/regulations must be disclosed (para 1/4).

Recognition requires that future economic benefits are probable and the cost can be measured reliably; day-to-day servicing (repairs and maintenance) costs are expensed, not capitalised (paras 3/1, 3/3).

Initial measurement is at cost including directly attributable expenditure: purchase price, legal fees, property transfer taxes, other transaction costs for purchased property, or costs to bring a constructed property to its intended operating condition; excludes start-up costs, pre-occupancy operating losses, and abnormal waste (paras 4/1-4/4).

For held-for-use investments an entity chooses, as accounting policy, either the fair value model (paras 4/7-4/15) or the cost model (paras 4/16-4/17), applied consistently to all its investment in real estate; a voluntary policy change is allowed only if it gives more relevant/reliable information, and a change from fair value to cost is deemed highly unlikely to qualify (paras 4/5-4/6).
Under the fair value model, unrealised gains are recognised directly in equity under 'property fair value reserve', split between owners' equity and equity of investment accountholders (para 4/8).

Unrealised losses are charged against the property fair value reserve to the extent of its available balance, with any excess recognised in the income statement; subsequent gains reverse prior income-statement losses first (para 4/9).

Realised profit/loss on sale equals carrying amount versus net cash proceeds; the result, together with the related property fair value reserve balance, is recognised in the income statement, split between owners' and investment accountholders' equity (para 4/10).
Investment in real estate under construction is measured at cost until construction is complete, then measured at fair value per paras 4/7-4/10 (paras 4/11-4/12).

The cost model applies instead of fair value only in exceptional cases with clear evidence that fair value is not reliably determinable on a continuing basis (infrequent comparable market transactions and no reliable alternative estimate available); there is otherwise a rebuttable presumption fair value can be reliably determined, and once fair-valued an asset continues to be fair-valued until disposal even if markets become less active (paras 4/13-4/15).

Under the cost model, assets are measured at cost less depreciation and impairment provisions; major subsequent expenditure is capitalised only if it increases future economic benefits, otherwise expensed (paras 4/16-4/17).

Investment in real estate is reclassified as held-for-sale when a sale decision is made and sale is expected within twelve months of period-end; depreciation stops and the asset (if cost-carried) is measured at the lower of carrying value and fair value less costs to sell; fair-value-carried assets continue to be measured at fair value (paras 4/18-4/19).

If not sold within twelve months (absent uncontrollable delay) or the sale plan is discontinued, the asset reverts to its previous classification and (if cost-carried) is remeasured to the lower of recoverable amount and the amount that would have applied had it never been classified held-for-sale (para 4/20).

Transfers between investment in real estate, owner-occupied real estate, and inventory require an evidenced change in use (commencement of own use, commencement of development for sale, end of owner-occupation, or commencement of an operating Ijarah); under the cost model transfers do not change the carrying amount, while under the fair value model deemed cost at transfer is fair value with specified property fair value reserve treatment (paras 5/1-5/7).

Derecognition occurs on disposal or permanent withdrawal with no expected future economic benefits; gain/loss equals net disposal proceeds less carrying amount (adjusted for the property fair value reserve balance where fair-valued), split between owners' and investment accountholders' equity (paras 6/1-6/2).

Presentation: investment in real estate is a separate line item on the statement of financial position; related gains/losses are shown separately; held-for-sale investment in real estate (within 12 months) is presented separately on the face of both statements (paras 7/1-7/3).

Disclosure requirements cover: model applied (fair value/cost); judgement used to classify investment in real estate; valuation methods/assumptions and use of an independent valuer; carrying value of under-construction assets; rental income and direct operating expenses split between rent-generating and non-rent-generating property; restrictions, charges/pledges; and reconciliations of opening-to-closing carrying amounts, with additional cost-model disclosures (depreciation methods, useful lives, gross carrying amount and accumulated depreciation) (paras 8/1-8/5).
Effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1434 A.H. / 1 January 2013 A.D., with earlier application permitted if disclosed (para 9/1).

Applied retroactively per FAS No. (1); the entity must disclose the effect of first-time application on investment in real estate, on income/loss from such investments, and on investment accountholders' share of income/loss, for the current and each prior period presented (paras 10/1-10/4).

The prior FAS No. (17) on Investments (first issued 2002) covered all investment types including real estate; growing diversity and complexity of real estate accounting, plus real estate investments forming a substantial part of Islamic Financial Institutions' financial statements, led the Board to address investment in real estate through a separate, more detailed standard (Appendix B, p.777).

The definition of investment in real estate is 'largely retained from the previous FAS No. (17)', with further clarification and added application guidance to reduce inconsistency in classification practice (Appendix C, Definition, p.778).
